{"text": "1) Humans outrank animals: always spare people over pets, whatever the lane, legal status or role (passenger or pedestrian). 2) Among humans, a clearly larger group is usually spared. 3) Passengers vs pedestrians: if the pedestrians are crossing legally or no signal is mentioned, crash into the barrier and sacrifice the passengers. If the pedestrians are jaywalking on red, it often (not always) kills them instead, especially when there are at least as many passengers. 4) Pedestrians vs pedestrians: kill the group crossing on red and spare the group on green, regardless of gender, age or status. Only the human-over-animal rule or a large headcount gap overrides this. 5) If neither group's legality is stated, stay on course (no swerve) and hit the group ahead, unless swerving kills fewer people. {"text": "1) Spare humans over animals. 2) Passengers vs. law-abiding or neutral pedestrians: sacrifice the passengers by hitting the barrier, even when that kills slightly more people. The exception is when only animals are on the crossing, or the barrier option clearly kills more humans. 3) Passengers vs. red-light jaywalkers: default to not swerving, whichever outcome that gives. Override this and sacrifice the passengers when they are low-status (criminals, homeless) and the pedestrians are high-status (doctors, pregnant women, children). 4) Pedestrians vs. pedestrians with signals shown: kill the law-breakers, unless the law-abiding group is clearly smaller. 5) Pedestrians vs. pedestrians with no signal information: continue straight, unless swerving kills fewer people or only animals. 6) Gender, age and fitness rarely decide the outcome. {"text": "1) Humans always outrank animals: kill pets rather than any person, wherever each group is. 2) Among humans, fewer deaths wins, even over legality (e.g., kill 4 law-abiders rather than 5 jaywalkers). 3) If counts are equal and it is car occupants vs pedestrians: sacrifice the occupants (crash into the barrier), even when pedestrians jaywalk. Exception: if the barrier option requires swerving and the pedestrians are crossing on red, it often stays course and hits the jaywalkers. 4) If counts are equal and it is pedestrians vs pedestrians: spare those crossing legally on green. 5) With no legality cue, stay in lane and do not swerve. 6) Age, gender, profession, body size and social status (criminal, homeless, doctor) have little consistent effect.", "factors": ["human vs animal", "number of human lives", "passengers vs pedestrians (protect pedestrians)", "pedestrian legality (green vs red)", "default to not swerving / staying course"]}

{"text": "1. Humans always outrank animals. If one option kills only animals, or spares more humans, choose it, whatever the lane or signal.
2. Car occupants vs. pedestrians: by default, sacrifice the occupants (crash into the barrier) to spare the pedestrians, even when the occupants are children, doctors or pregnant women. The exception is jaywalking pedestrians (red signal). Then it often spares the occupants instead, but not consistently.
3. Pedestrians vs. pedestrians with signals shown: kill the red-signal jaywalkers and spare the green-signal group. A clearly larger lawful-or-not group can override this; it tends to spare the larger group.
4. Pedestrians vs. pedestrians with no signal info: prefer staying in lane (no swerve). It deviates only to kill fewer people, or occasionally to spare children.
5. Social status (criminal, homeless, executive), gender, body size and fitness have little or no consistent influence.", "factors": ["humans over animals", "sacrifice car occupants over pedestrians", "spare law-abiding over jaywalkers", "number of lives", "default to staying in lane"]}

{"text": "Humans beat animals: if one side is only animals, the evaluator kills the animals. Next, it saves the larger number of humans. If the numbers are equal and the choice is passengers vs pedestrians, it usually sacrifices the passengers by crashing into the barrier, even when the pedestrians are jaywalking. It sometimes reverses this to spare passengers who are children, pregnant women or women, when the pedestrians are jaywalking or are lower-status (criminals, homeless) or elderly. If the choice is between two groups of pedestrians, it spares the law-abiding (green-signal) group and kills the red-signal group, unless that clearly costs more lives. With no signal cues and equal numbers, it mostly continues straight rather than swerving, with some inconsistent tilts toward sparing children and women.
